title: Why Latent Actions Fail, and How to Prevent It
claim: Standard latent-action learning fails through leakage and noise-sensitive features; three targeted remedies prevent these failures.
layout: 2 halves, left-to-right: failure cases left, remedy diagram plus numbered list right
description: The figure has two halves under emoji-headed titles. The left half, 'Why Latent Actions Fail?' with a sad emoji, holds two boxed panels. The first, 'Future leakage', shows an encoder-decoder diagram. Two frames feed the encoder, which produces a latent z. A red curved 'Shortcut' arrow runs from the future frame straight to z, while a dotted 'Ignore' arrow points at the decoder. The second panel, 'Noise-sensitive vision feature', compares a Pixel feature map (red border) with a DINOv2 feature map (green border). The right half, 'How to Prevent Failure?' with a smiling emoji, shows an encoder-decoder diagram. Frames pass through feature extractors f to give o and o'. Numbered markers 1 to 3 mark the remedy points: y supervision on z, and a swapped latent z-tilde. Gray boxes list the three remedies. Lavender blocks are the main visual anchor.
caption: Failure modes and remedies for latent action learning. (Left) Future leakage and noise-sensitive visual features hinder the learning of action-centric latent representations. (Right) Our theoretical analysis explains why three remedies work: a noise-robust vision encoder, supervision with a noise-robust target y, and latent action swapping across exogenous states.
abstract: Latent action models (LAMs) aim to learn action-like representations from unlabeled videos by compressing frame-to-frame changes. The frames of in-the-wild videos, however, contain not only the agent's own state but exogenous state such as background clutter. Since the exogenous state introduces changes unrelated to actions, it hinders reliable latent action learning. This paper investigates this problem analytically by extending a linear LAM framework to explicitly model exogenous state. Our analysis reveals two insights: (1) minimizing the standard reconstruction objective produces latent actions that encode exogenous information from future observation; and (2) learning in a representation space that focuses on endogenous components is a key to mitigating the interference of noise. We further show that previously proposed auxiliary objectives, such as action-supervision, provably encourage latent actions to be consistent across exogenous states. These findings are validated through experiments on both linear and nonlinear LAMs, providing a unified theoretical analysis of how exogenous state hinders latent action learning and why common remedies work.
